section_1.title: From Concrete to Abstract: The Prerequisite
section_1.content: Briefly review 2D/3D vectors as arrows with magnitude and direction. Introduce the transition: what if our 'vectors' aren't arrows, but functions or polynomials? Define a vector space as a 'playground' where we only care about two operations: Addition and Scalar Multiplication, provided they obey 8 specific rules (axioms).
section_1.example: Visualize a 2D plane arrow transforming into a smooth mathematical function curve, showing that both follow the same algebraic 'rules of the road'.

section_2.title: The 8 Axioms: Defining the Rules of the Playground
section_2.content: Categorize the 8 axioms into two groups: Closure (staying in the space) and Structure (distributivity, associativity, and identity). Use a simplified visual checklist to emphasize that any set, regardless of what its members look like, is a 'Vector Space' if it satisfies these properties.
section_2.example: Imagine a 'Vector Animal Shelter': Dogs (vectors) can be added (combined) and scaled (grown/shrunk). As long as adding two dogs doesn't result in a cat, the shelter follows the 'Closure' rule.

section_3.title: Testing the Concept: Polynomials as Vectors
section_3.content: Apply the theory to the space of polynomials P2. Show how adding (x^2 + x) + (2x + 1) behaves exactly like adding coordinates (1,1,0) + (0,2,1). This highlights the 'Isomorphism'—that the internal structure is identical to simple vectors.
section_3.example: An animation showing polynomial coefficients shifting into grid coordinates on a graph, proving that x^2 + x acts exactly like a 3D coordinate vector.

section_4.title: Application: Why Abstract Matters
section_4.content: Conclude by explaining that by abstracting vectors, we can solve complex real-world problems (like sound processing or quantum mechanics) using the same simple linear algebra we use for 3D graphics.
section_4.example: A visual representation of an audio wave (a vector in an infinite-dimensional space) being manipulated by the same rules as a simple arrow on a coordinate plane.
